Plain English — Round numbers like “1,000 days” carry no legal or administrative meaning; they are a calendar coincidence that both a government and its opposition treat as a free news hook. Mechanics — Indian governments and oppositions both maintain running day-counts of an administration’s term (100 days, 500 days, 1,000 days, and so on) specifically to have a ready-made occasion for a scorecard. Incentives — For the government, the date is a chance to control the narrative with its own numbers first; for the opposition, it is a chance to force a comparison on a day the government cannot avoid public attention. Numbers — 1,000 days is roughly 2 years 9 months — a little under a third of a typical 5-year term, making it an early-to-midpoint checkpoint, not a final verdict. S2 · The government’s own report card Civil Supplies Minister N Uttam Kumar Reddy released a document titled “1,000 Days of Welfare and Development — Telangana Report Card,” framing the period as a shift from “family rule to people’s rule” and a “restoration of democracy” after BRS’s decade in office. Plain English — A senior minister, not the Chief Minister himself, was chosen to release the document — a common practice that lets the CM stay above the specifics while a colleague carries the messaging. Mechanics — The “family rule” framing is a direct jab at BRS, which was founded and long led by the Rao family (K Chandrashekar Rao as Chief Minister, his son K T Rama Rao and daughter K Kavitha both holding senior party and government roles during BRS’s decade in power). Incentives — Releasing a self-authored report card first, before the opposition can define the narrative, is standard political sequencing — whoever publishes numbers first often gets quoted as the baseline, even if a rival immediately disputes them. Numbers — No dedicated figures in this fact; the numbers arrive in S3. S3 · The government’s headline numbers The report card cites per-capita income of Rs 4,18,931 for 2025-26 (said to be roughly 91% above the national average); farm loan waivers of up to Rs 2 lakh for about 25 lakh farming families; over Rs 36,000 crore disbursed under the Rythu Bharosa farmer-support scheme; roughly 70,000 government jobs filled; Telangana overtaking Punjab as India’s top paddy producer with 81.12 lakh tonnes procured; more than 335 crore free bus trips for women under the Mahalakshmi scheme; free electricity up to 200 units for 53 lakh families under Gruha Jyothi; and Rs 500 cooking-gas cylinders for 43 lakh families. Plain English — This is a long list of welfare-delivery numbers, each measuring how much the government spent or gave away, not independently how much better off any single family actually is. Mechanics — Every one of these numbers comes from the government’s own departments, released in the government’s own report — they are self-reported administrative statistics, not figures independently audited or verified by a third party such as the CAG at the time of release. Incentives — Big, precise-looking numbers (91% above national average; 81.12 lakh tonnes) read as more credible than round ones — a well-known messaging technique, though precision is not the same as independent verification. Numbers — Rs 36,000 crore under Rythu Bharosa alone is a very large sum — for comparison, it is close to double what the entire Raidurg land-auction programme has raised for the state government this year (roughly Rs 2,833 crore from the two most recent Raidurg sales combined, covered in earlier editions) — showing how much bigger welfare spending is than one-off land-sale revenue as a share of the state’s finances. S4 · The Moosarambagh bridge speech and the debate challenge On Monday evening (31 August), Chief Minister Revanth Reddy inaugurated a new high-level bridge over the Musi river at Moosarambagh, and used the platform to publicly challenge former Chief Minister K Chandrashekar Rao (KCR) to a floor debate in the Assembly, comparing Congress’s 1,000 days against BRS’s 10 years in power, once the Monsoon Session opens on 7 September. Plain English — The Chief Minister chose a freshly-built piece of public infrastructure as the backdrop for a direct political taunt at his predecessor. Mechanics — An Assembly “debate” challenge is more theatre than a real procedural mechanism — there is no rule that forces KCR, who is not currently attending sessions, to show up and answer; it is a rhetorical dare designed to be reported, not necessarily accepted. Incentives — By tying the challenge to a bridge inauguration, the CM gets two news events in one — a delivered-infrastructure photo-op plus a political jab — while knowing KCR is unlikely to actually appear and debate. Numbers — No new figures in this fact. S5 · The specific charges against KCR’s absence Revanth Reddy said KCR has “confined himself to his farmhouse,” has not attended a single Assembly session in the 1,000 days since losing power, drew Rs 1.24 crore in salary as a sitting MLA during that period, while the state spent about Rs 22 crore on his security and official facilities as former Chief Minister. Plain English — The CM is arguing that KCR keeps drawing a legislator’s pay and a former-CM’s security cover while doing none of the public-facing legislative work either role implies. Mechanics — In India, a sitting MLA continues to draw salary and allowances regardless of attendance (there is no automatic pay cut for absenteeism), and a former Chief Minister is entitled to a standard security and facilities package under state protocol rules — both are lawful entitlements, not misuse, which is exactly why this is a political argument about optics, not a legal or procedural violation. Incentives — Framing a legal entitlement as wasteful is a common way to make an opponent’s inaction sound like a scandal, even when nothing about it breaks any rule. Numbers — Rs 1.24 crore in salary and roughly Rs 22 crore in state-funded security/facilities over 1,000 days — these are the CM’s own claimed figures, not yet independently corroborated by an official disclosure or RTI response in the reporting reviewed, so treat them as one side’s asserted numbers. S6 · Six days of dharnas demanding KCR’s resignation Revanth Reddy called for six days of Congress-led dharnas (sit-in protests) demanding KCR’s resignation as MLA, starting Tuesday 1 September — the same day BRS was staging its own counter-campaign launch. Plain English — The ruling party is running a street-protest campaign against the very opposition leader whose party is simultaneously protesting against the ruling party — both sides are in the streets on the same days. Mechanics — A sitting MLA cannot be legally forced to resign by public protest alone; resignation demands like this function purely as pressure and messaging, similar to the “resign immediately” demand AIMIM made of expelled MLC Mirza Rahmath Baig, covered elsewhere in this edition — a request, not an enforceable outcome. Incentives — Matching the opposition’s protest calendar day-for-day denies BRS a clear run at dominating the news cycle around the 1,000-day milestone. Numbers — Six days, timed to overlap almost exactly with BRS’s own announced 2–8 September campaign window (S7). S7 · BRS’s rival chargesheet BRS working president K T Rama Rao (KTR) released a political “chargesheet” against the Congress government at Telangana Bhavan on 1 September, alleging the government has failed to fulfil even a single one of 420 promises, 13 declarations and six guarantees it originally pledged to deliver within its first 100 days in office. Plain English — BRS is arguing that Congress’s own original campaign promises, not BRS’s standards, are the yardstick Congress should be judged against — and that on that yardstick, three years on, nothing has been delivered. Mechanics — A political “chargesheet” borrows the language of a criminal charge document but carries no legal force whatsoever — it cannot be filed in any court and creates no legal liability; it is campaign material, formatted to look authoritative. Incentives — Choosing the same 1 September date as the government’s own milestone, and the same venue-style formality (a press conference at party headquarters) as a government release, is deliberate mirroring — BRS wants its document treated with the same weight as the government’s. Numbers — “Zero of 420” is BRS’s own claim and has not been independently verified fact-by-fact in the reporting available; as of this research, only the pre-event announcement of the chargesheet’s existence was confirmed, not a verified line-by-line account of its actual content on the day, so treat the “420 promises” figure as BRS’s framing, not an audited count. S8 · The week-long BRS campaign, including a land-specific protest Following the chargesheet release, BRS has planned a week-long campaign (2–8 September): constituency-level dharnas over the “six guarantees” on 2 September, the display of 420-foot-long banners and “Baaki Cards” (due/debt cards) listing unmet promises, farmer conferences across the state on 3 September covering agriculture, irrigation, power supply, urea shortages and crop insurance, and — per this edition’s earlier coverage — a protest specifically over the Section 22A prohibited-lands issue also timed to 3 September. Plain English — This is not one protest but a coordinated, multi-day statewide campaign with different themes assigned to different days, run like a mini election campaign rather than a single rally. Mechanics — Section 22A is the Telangana rule under which sub-registrars must refuse to register land on a “prohibited” list — a list that has wrongly swept up genuine private property in past months (covered in this edition’s Concept Library and earlier Deep Dives); folding a land-registration grievance into a broader “broken promises” campaign lets BRS attach a concrete, personally-felt harm (a frozen property) to an otherwise abstract political argument. Incentives — Farmer conferences and a land-registration protest both target rural and landowning voters specifically — a signal that BRS sees land and agriculture grievances as its strongest available wedge against Congress right now. Numbers — A 420-foot banner is a deliberate visual pun on the “420 promises” claim — one foot of banner per allegedly broken promise. S9 · The government’s own newspaper is not simply cheerleading Telangana Today published its own analytical piece the same evening (31 August, 6:37 PM) pushing back on parts of the government’s report card — noting that TIMS hospital projects being credited to Congress were largely built under the previous BRS government; that the Regional Ring Road has shown no progress in 30 months; that Warangal airport plans remain stalled; and that zero “Young India Integrated Residential Schools” have been built despite a promise of one per Assembly constituency. Plain English — Even before BRS’s formal chargesheet landed, at least one Telangana outlet had already independently flagged gaps between the government’s claims and the state of specific stalled projects. Mechanics — This is ordinary accountability journalism — comparing a government’s own claimed timeline against visible, checkable facts on the ground (has a road been built, has an airport plan moved, have schools opened) — not itself a partisan attack. Incentives — A same-day critical piece from a mainstream outlet, appearing independently of BRS’s own messaging, is more credible corroboration of specific gaps (RRR, Warangal airport, the residential schools) than either party’s own claims about the other. Numbers — “Zero of one-per-constituency” Young India schools, against however many of Telangana’s roughly 119 Assembly constituencies were promised one — a concrete, checkable shortfall distinct from the more rhetorical “420 promises” framing. S10 · The High Court’s land-loser question The same Telangana Today piece noted that a Telangana High Court judge, Justice N V Shravan Kumar, had separately questioned why the government found the funds to resume marriage-aid (Kalyana Lakshmi/Shaadi Mubarak-style) payments while people whose land had already been acquired for government projects were still waiting on their compensation. Plain English — A judge, hearing an unrelated case, pointedly asked why the government pays for one type of welfare promptly while people who gave up their land for public projects are left waiting to be paid what they are legally owed. Mechanics — This is a judicial observation made in passing during a hearing, not a formal court order or ruling — it carries no binding legal force and creates no enforceable deadline, but it is a rare instance of an independent, non-partisan voice raising the exact same prioritisation question both political parties have every incentive to avoid: is welfare spending being prioritised over legal compensation debts? Incentives — Neither Congress (which wants credit for welfare delivery) nor BRS (whose own government also had unresolved land-compensation cases) has an obvious incentive to spotlight this specific question, which is exactly why it is easy for it to get buried under the louder report-card-versus-chargesheet fight. Numbers — No specific compensation figure or land-loser count was available in the reporting reviewed — this is flagged as an open question, not a quantified scandal, and is worth tracking for a specific number in a future edition. Namasthe Telangana, this edition’s flagged BRS-aligned outlet, was checked for its framing of the chargesheet call but added no additional independently-verifiable facts beyond what the other outlets carried. 3 · Glossary — every term, simply 1,000 days (as a political milestone) A round-number count of a government’s time in office, with no legal significance, used as an occasion for both self-praise and opposition attack. Example: a company celebrating “10 years in business” with a sale — the number itself changes nothing, but it’s a convenient hook for a message. Report card (political) A government’s own self-graded summary of what it has achieved, published by the government itself rather than an independent body. Example: like a student writing their own school report card — informative, but you’d still want the teacher’s version too. Chargesheet (political, as used here) An opposition party’s list of a government’s alleged failures, borrowing the name of a criminal-court document but carrying no legal force. Example: a competitor’s attack ad listing everything wrong with a rival product — persuasive marketing, not a court finding. Rythu Bharosa Telangana’s scheme paying farmers a fixed per-acre cash amount each season to support cultivation costs, regardless of what crop they grow. Example: like a flat annual stipend a farmer gets just for having land under cultivation, on top of whatever they earn selling the crop. Mahalakshmi scheme A Telangana scheme letting women travel free on state-run (TGSRTC) buses. Example: a free public-transport pass, but only for women and only on government buses, not private ones. Gruha Jyothi A Telangana scheme giving eligible households free electricity up to a monthly usage cap (up to 200 units, per the report card). Example: like your electricity bill being waived entirely as long as you stay under a set usage limit each month. Per-capita income The average income per person in a region, calculated by dividing total economic output by population — a broad average that says nothing about how income is actually distributed between rich and poor. Example: if one person earns Rs 100 and nine earn Rs 0, the “per-capita income” of the group is still Rs 10 each, even though nine people have nothing. Assembly (Legislative Assembly) Telangana’s state legislature, where elected MLAs debate and pass laws and budgets. Example: like a state-level parliament; Telangana’s has about 119 elected members. MLA (Member of the Legislative Assembly) An elected representative in a state’s Assembly, representing one constituency. Example: the state-level equivalent of a Member of Parliament, but for a single state rather than the whole country. Dharna A sit-in style protest, typically peaceful, where demonstrators occupy a public space to press a demand and draw press attention. Example: a workplace sit-in, but staged in front of a government building instead of an office. Section 22A (Telangana Registration Act) The rule under which certain survey numbers are placed on a “prohibited” list that sub-registrars must refuse to register — meant to block government/temple/ceiling-surplus land sales, but prone to wrongly trapping genuine private property (fully explained in this edition’s Concept Library). Example: like a bank freezing an account by mistake because a similar account number was flagged for fraud — the freeze is real even when the underlying reason is a clerical error. CAG (Comptroller and Auditor General) India’s independent constitutional auditor of government accounts at both the central and state level — not part of any government department, and its reports are the closest thing to a neutral financial referee on claims like the ones in today’s report card. Example: like an external auditor a company is legally required to use, rather than checking its own books. High Court The highest court within a single Indian state (Telangana’s sits in Hyderabad), one level below the Supreme Court of India. Example: a state-level appellate court, roughly analogous to a US state supreme court. Land acquisition compensation The payment the government legally owes a landowner when it takes their land for a public project (a road, a bridge, an irrigation canal). Example: like a compulsory purchase in other countries — the government can take the land, but the law requires it to pay a set price for doing so, and delay in that payment is itself a legal grievance. Musi river / Musi Riverfront The river running through Hyderabad, currently the subject of a large state government redevelopment programme (the Musi Riverfront project, covered in earlier editions) that includes new bridges such as the one inaugurated at Moosarambagh. Beneath the dueling-numbers surface, the deeper forces are familiar to any state that has just changed ruling parties: a new government needs three years of delivery to look credible before the next election cycle begins to loom, while an opposition that lost power decisively needs to prove it is still relevant without the daily visibility that governing provides. Both parties are also managing internal pressures that rarely make the milestone headlines — Congress is simultaneously handling the Konda Surekha Cabinet crisis (covered elsewhere in this edition), while BRS is managing its own KCR-succession question in the background, with KTR the visible face of a party whose founder has become steadily less publicly active. What a ten-year Telangana political follower knows, that a first-time reader of today’s headlines might not: this exact report-card-versus-chargesheet pattern repeats at every major milestone in Indian state politics, and the specific numbers rarely settle anything on their own — what tends to actually move public opinion, over the following weeks, is whichever side’s claims survive contact with an independent check, such as a CAG report, a court observation, or a RERA/land-registration outcome that ordinary people can verify against their own experience. 5 · So what — stakes and consequences The government wins if its report card’s big numbers (jobs filled, farm support disbursed, free electricity and bus travel delivered) stick in public memory more than BRS’s “420 promises” framing — a battle of which side’s big number is more memorable, not necessarily which side is more accurate. BRS wins if its chargesheet, plus Telangana Today’s independent flags on stalled projects (RRR, Warangal airport, Young India schools), combine to make “undelivered” the more credible frame heading into the Assembly session and, eventually, the next election cycle. The quieter loser, so far, is whoever is still waiting on land-acquisition compensation — a group neither party’s messaging machine has any strong incentive to spotlight, and the one group a High Court judge, entirely outside the political fight, chose to raise unprompted. Watch for: (1) whether KCR actually appears for any Assembly-floor exchange after 7 September, or whether the “debate challenge” quietly drops after its news cycle passes — likelihood: KCR appearing is low, given his reported pattern of non-attendance; (2) whether BRS’s Section 22A protest on 3 September produces any concrete government response beyond the existing committee process — moderate likelihood, given the committee’s own 15-day clearance deadline lands around the same window; (3) whether any outlet or RTI response ever produces a verified land-loser compensation figure responding to Justice Shravan Kumar’s question — lower likelihood in the short term, since neither party benefits from surfacing it, but worth checking again in a future edition. What this means for you: for Hyderabad/Telangana real estate directly, the most durable thread inside today’s noise is the Section 22A protest folded into BRS’s campaign and the High Court’s land-compensation question — both point to land registration and acquisition payment delays as a live, unresolved risk category, regardless of which party’s messaging wins the news cycle. For business and investment more broadly, today’s episode is a reminder that self-reported government statistics (from either a ruling party’s report card or an opposition’s chargesheet) should be treated as advocacy until corroborated by an independent source like the CAG, a court, or a regulator such as TG-RERA. The beginner mistake here is treating either the report card or the chargesheet as the real story; the sharper read is to watch the one paragraph in Telangana Today’s independent piece and the one line from a High Court judge — the two facts in this whole episode that neither political party chose to put there themselves. 6 · The 20% that gives you 100% — your keep-forever map On the day Telangana’s Congress government completed 1,000 days in office, it published its own report card of welfare delivery, and the opposition BRS published a rival chargesheet claiming zero of 420 original promises had been kept — both released the same day, both self-authored, both unaudited at the point of release. The Chief Minister used a bridge inauguration to challenge his predecessor to a public debate that the predecessor is unlikely to accept. The one genuinely independent voice in the entire episode belonged to a High Court judge, who asked in passing why land-acquisition compensation was still unpaid while other welfare spending had resumed. 2026-09-01|ls-scams: Common land scams in India and how to protect yourself Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Common Land Scams in India and How to Protect Yourself — 1acre.in Key Highlights Fraud thrives where records are scattered: ~95% of RoRs are computerised, but only ~68% of cadastral maps. The deadliest scam is the LEGAL-LOOKING one: registered deeds on assigned land are void — registration proves nothing. Seven patterns cover most of the market: forged titles, restricted land, duplicate sales, PoA abuse, encroachment, benami, fake pre-launch schemes. The defence is always the same: pull the records YOURSELF — RoR, EC, prohibited list, title chain. Remote buyers and absentee owners are the favourite targets. Why India’s land market attracts so much fraud Fraud grows wherever information is scarce and checking is hard. India’s records are digitising UNEVENLY — about 95% of Records of Rights computerised but only 68% of cadastral maps, with some districts still on ageing paper — and every state runs its own system. The favourite victims: buyers unfamiliar with local revenue records, people purchasing remotely, and plots whose owners are absent or unaware something is being sold in their name. The most devastating one: restricted land sold as normal Certain land legally CANNOT be freely sold: government-assigned land, tribal land, ceiling-surplus land, endowment (temple) land, forest land. The scam: a legitimate-looking registered document, payment made, registration completed — and years or decades later the government reclaims the land because it was assigned all along. Buyer loses land, money and everything built on it. The legal trap: the prohibited-list mechanism (Section 22-A) only BLOCKS registration of parcels actually on the Collector’s list — unlisted assigned parcels register fine — but the transfer-ban law voids the sale regardless of what any registrar accepted. So: check the prohibited register AND the revenue record’s remarks, always. Seven scams to know 1) Title fraud and forged documents — the most widespread: a fraudster forges papers, poses as owner or PoA holder, sells land that is not theirs; forged paper carries zero legal weight, which is why the CHAIN matters more than the current deed. 2) Restricted-land sales — as above. 3) Duplicate sales — one plot sold to two or more buyers, exploiting slow registration; not a pure first-to-register race (a deed relates back to its execution date under Section 47), but the genuinely prior sale usually prevails and everyone else litigates. 4) PoA abuse — forged, expired or revoked PoAs used to sell without the owner’s knowledge; an unregistered PoA, or one not clearly authorising sale, is a warning. 5) Encroachment folded in — the boundary shown quietly includes government or neighbouring land; good title to part, nothing on the rest; a boundary survey catches it. 6) Benami deals — property in someone else’s name to hide the real buyer; illegal under the 2016 Benami law, with confiscation and up to seven years’ rigorous imprisonment. 7) Fake pre-launch schemes — units sold in unapproved projects with assured-return promises backed by post-dated cheques that bounce; RERA bars selling before registration, so a pre-launch pitch WITHOUT a RERA number is the tell. Definition — Benami transaction: a purchase held in a name-lender’s name while someone else pays and controls it. Since the 2016 amendment the property can be confiscated outright — buyer-side participation is itself the crime. Red flags and what they mean Warning sign What it usually means What to do Price well below market Defect the seller knows and you don’t Slow down; the discount IS the disclosure Pressure to close fast Verification window being shortened deliberately Never pay before checks complete Seller supplies all documents, resists your own EC pull Papers may be curated or forged Pull EC and RoR yourself from official sources Sale via PoA, owner unreachable Possible PoA abuse or a dead/unaware principal Meet or video-verify the owner; check PoA registration “Registration will fix everything” Confusing registration with valid title Remember: void transfers register too No RERA number on a project pitch Unapproved / pre-launch scheme Verify on the state RERA portal before any token Documents to check before any purchase ☐ Title + sale deed — seller’s name matches the record; chain traced 30 years. ☐ Record of Rights — owner, classification, mutation history, restriction remarks. ☐ EC — pulled by YOU from the sub-registrar; never the seller’s copy. ☐ Land use / conversion — classification confirmed; conversion completed if it was agricultural. ☐ Mutation — updated, no restriction notes. ☐ Tax receipts — dues attach to the LAND, not the old owner. ☐ RERA — verified on the portal for any plotted or builder project. ☐ PoA, if involved — authorises sale, registered where required, traceable to the real owner. What maps can and cannot catch Survey-number maps, master-plan overlays and satellite imagery catch boundary and zoning mismatches — whether the parcel’s ground reality matches the deed, and whether it sits in a restricted zone — before a site visit. They cannot read a title chain, tell a forged deed from a genuine one, or check the prohibited list. That work stays with the sub-registrar’s records and a revenue-law advocate. Quick answers (FAQ) Most common scam? Title fraud with forged documents. How do I know if land has transfer restrictions? RoR remarks + the state’s prohibited-property register. Can I buy through a PoA? Yes, with independent verification of the PoA and the principal — PoA sales are not inherently illegitimate. What if I unknowingly bought restricted land? The transfer is void; get a revenue advocate immediately. Is RERA-registered land always safe? Safer — but RERA checks the project, not the title chain; do both. How to report fraud? Police complaint (EOW for large frauds) + civil suit; registration of a case does not undo the transfer, so prevention is the real remedy. Bottom line Nearly every land scam succeeds at the same moment: when the buyer accepts someone else’s paperwork instead of pulling their own. RoR, EC, prohibited list, 30-year chain, boundary survey — five self-service checks defeat all seven scams. For you: Your buyers fear exactly this list — which makes it your marketing. A venture that publishes its own verification file (chain, EC, prohibited-list clearance, DTCP approval) sells trust the unorganised market cannot. Internally: rule — no landowner conversation advances until the RoR and prohibited-list check are done, however warm the introduction. The Encumbrance Certificate, pulled for 15–30 years, is the first filter for hidden loans and old claims. eCourts and the NJDG let you search pending cases free — but a wrong spelling can hide the case. Lis pendens binds a new buyer to a pending case’s outcome even if nobody told them it existed. Revenue-court disputes and old village claims are often NOT online — a physical visit still counts. What checking for disputes actually means There is a difference between a title that LOOKS fine and one that has been CHECKED. Land carries history the deed never shows: an old inheritance quarrel, a boundary shifted after a family split, a loan never cleared. A litigation check confirms — through independent sources, never the seller’s word — that none of this is unresolved. Two different searches get confused: the EC tracks registered financial claims; a court search tracks live litigation. A property can be clean on one and dirty on the other. What a proper check covers Encumbrance history — loans, mortgages, claims, from the SRO. Court cases — anything involving the owner or the property, via eCourts and the NJDG. Ownership and survey records — mutation entries cross-checked against the deed. Unrecorded local disputes — boundary and revenue matters not yet digital. The neighbours — who usually know about a fight before any court does. Why the check must happen before you pay anything Land fights make up a striking share of India’s pending civil cases, tracing to a few causes: contested inheritance, forged papers, unclear titles, encroachment. A seller with a pending case usually will not mention it. The check matters at three moments: before the offer, before any advance, and before registration — each later stage makes a discovered defect more expensive. Definition — Lis pendens: “suit pending”. Once litigation over land is on foot, whoever buys the land inherits the case’s outcome — knowledge or ignorance makes no difference. The law assumes you searched. Start with the Encumbrance Certificate Ask for at least 15 years, ideally 30 — a spotless five-year EC says nothing about a fifteen-year-old dispute that never resolved. Read it for court attachments, unreleased liens, and windows where entries abruptly stop; a gap is a question, not a quirk. Then search eCourts and the NJDG Both portals cover District and High Courts, searchable by party name, case number or type — free. Search the owner’s name in every reasonable variation (initials, spellings), the FAMILY’S names, and past owners’ names from the chain. A nil result under one spelling proves only that spelling. Example: A buyer near Shamshabad stopped at a clean EC. The seller’s sister’s partition suit was two minutes away on eCourts — under HER name. The court notice arrived after his registration; lis pendens did the rest. Red flags — what they usually mean, what to do Red flag What it usually means What to do EC entries suddenly stop A dispute or transaction may have been kept off the record Ask the SRO for a written explanation of the gap eCourts returns nothing at all The case may sit under a name variant Re-search with initials and past owners’ names Seller resists the full-period EC Possibly avoiding an older entry Insist on the 15–30 year window — non-negotiable Neighbours mention a fight the seller did not Local knowledge runs ahead of filings Visit the tahsildar; investigate before any advance Title changed hands fast and often Rapid resales can be laundering a defect Trace and check each prior owner in the chain The physical checks documents cannot replace Revenue-court records — at the tahsildar or sub-divisional office — are mostly not digitised; someone must go and look. Neighbours help more than expected. For anything beyond a small purchase, a lawyer running the full search is cheap against the alternative. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ EC for 15–30 years. ☐ eCourts + NJDG searched under every reasonable name variation. ☐ Ownership and survey details cross-checked on the state portal. ☐ SRO and revenue office visited for what is not online. ☐ Neighbours asked about disputes and boundaries. ☐ Lawyer’s full search before any advance. Quick answers (FAQ) Can I search property litigation online free? Yes — eCourts and NJDG. Do all disputes show there? No — revenue matters and fresh village fights often exist offline first. What if I unknowingly buy disputed land? Lis pendens binds you to the outcome; your recourse is against the seller — which is why the check precedes the money. How far back should the EC go? 30 years where possible; 15 as the floor. Bottom line Disputes rarely announce themselves; they sit in old entries and filings the seller has no reason to mention. A few hours across the EC, eCourts and one village visit cost almost nothing against untangling a case later. Market value for land runs on registered comparables, frontage, road access and zone. The two numbers, defined Guideline value (circle rate, ready-reckoner rate, unit rate — the name varies by state): the registration department’s benchmark valuation for each locality and land type, existing to stop parties under-declaring prices to dodge duty. The Income Tax Act sweeps all the local names into one term: the stamp duty value . Market value : what a willing buyer actually pays a willing seller — set by demand, not by notification. Duty runs on the higher number Duty is computed on the guideline value or the declared price, WHICHEVER IS HIGHER. Declaring a lower price does not help — where the declared figure falls below the benchmark, the department simply applies the benchmark. Exact rates vary by state; calculate with your jurisdiction’s numbers. The trap: buying below the guideline value Buying ABOVE the benchmark costs you duty; buying BELOW it can cost you INCOME TAX. Under Section 56(2)(x), where you buy immovable property for less than its stamp-duty value, the shortfall is treated as YOUR income under “Income from Other Sources” (subject to the tolerance band). A genuine bargain thus gets taxed as if the discount were a gift to you. One protective mechanism: where agreement and registration dates differ, the benchmark ON THE AGREEMENT DATE can be adopted — but only if part of the consideration moved by cheque, draft or electronic transfer on or before that date. A CASH token does not qualify. And states revise values periodically, so always verify the figure on the date that matters to YOUR transaction. Example: You agree a plot at ₹60 lakh in March by handshake; the state revises the guideline to ₹75 lakh in April; you register in June. The transfer mode of one token payment carried lakhs of consequence. What moves the guideline value Location does most of the work — established and fast-developing pockets carry higher benchmarks because demand is already on record. Then: zoning — what the land may legally be used for feeds the assessed band; infrastructure — a new road or transit line lifts the benchmark, but only at the NEXT revision; and revision frequency itself varies by state, which is why benchmarks drift from reality in both directions. What determines market value For land the drivers are physical and legal, not cosmetic: frontage and road width; corner position; whether the survey number matches the ground; the master-plan zone and whether conversion is complete; and above all, what comparable parcels nearby actually REGISTERED for — a different number from what they were advertised at.
